summary: This document defines a Relay Agent Identifier sub-option for the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Information option. It carries a value that uniquely identifies the relay agent within its administrative domain, normally set by an administrator. A relay agent can include it in DHCP messages it forwards.

eli5.summary: A helper passing messages along gets a name badge. The badge number lets everyone tell which helper passed a message on.

questions: what is the relay agent identifier sub-option

how does dhcp relay agent information work
subtitle: A name tag for DHCPv4 relay agents so servers can tell which relay a message came through.

tldr.problem: DHCP servers have no standard way to learn which relay agent forwarded a client's message, which matters for uses such as bulk lease queries and location-based configuration.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6925 defines the Relay Agent Identifier sub-option (code 12) for the Relay Agent Information option. It carries an administratively configured octet string that must be unique within the administrative domain.
tldr.outcome: Servers can tie leases and configuration to a specific relay device, provided administrators keep identifiers stable and unique.

facts.label: Uniqueness
facts.value: MUST be unique within the administrative domain

today: RFC 6925 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated, according to its metadata.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DHCPv4 (RFC 2131) hands out IP addresses and configuration to IPv4 clients. A relay agent receives broadcast messages from clients and forwards them to DHCP servers as unicast messages. Many relay agents add information before forwarding, using the Relay Agent Information option (RFC 3046). Servers that recognize that option echo it back in their replies.

RFC 6925 adds one more piece: the Relay Agent Identifier (Relay-ID) sub-option. It carries a sequence of octets meant to identify the relay agent uniquely within its administrative domain. Here, an administrative domain means all the DHCP servers and relay agents that communicate with each other.
sections.eli5: When a helper passes a note from a kid to the teacher, the helper can stick on a badge with their own number. Then the teacher knows which helper brought it.

sections.title: Why a Relay Identifier Helps
sections.content:
The RFC gives two example use cases. The first is bulk leasequery. A relay agent can ask DHCP servers for all the leases allocated through it, using the relay identifier. This use case is described in RFC 6926, which proposes enhancements to the Leasequery protocol (RFC 4388).

The second is industrial Ethernet. DHCP normally identifies clients by things like the Client-Identifier option or the chaddr field. In factory-floor networks, a device's role is often fixed and based on its location, so the point of attachment is a more useful identifier. A network element acting as relay agent can supply identifier information that a server uses as a client identifier, for example by combining a port/slot value with the Relay-ID of the network element.
sections.eli5: In a factory, what a machine does depends on where it is plugged in. The helper's badge number plus the plug number tells the server exactly which spot a message came from.

sections.title: The Sub-Option Format
sections.content:
The sub-option has three parts: the sub-option code SUBOPT_RELAY_ID, whose value is 12, a length octet, and the variable-length identifier.

The length is the number of octets in the sub-option, not counting the code and length fields themselves. The minimum length is one. The identifier is simply the identifying data; the RFC does not impose any internal structure on it.
sections.eli5: The badge has a label saying it is a badge, a number saying how long the name is, and then the name itself.

sections.title: Keeping the Identifier Stable
sections.content:
An identifier is only useful if it stays the same. A relay agent SHOULD use a single identifier value consistently, and SHOULD commit it to stable storage unless it can regenerate the value after a reboot.

The identifier needs to be present in every DHCP message type where the server uses it. A relay agent may not be able to add the Relay Agent Information option to all messages, such as RENEW messages sent as IP unicasts. Some deployments let the server keep associating the last relay identifier it saw with a lease being renewed. Others use the Server Identifier Override sub-option (RFC 5107) so the relay can insert the option into all relayed messages.

Replacement matters too. If a relay device fails or is upgraded, the new device may need to present the same identifier as the old one. So a relay agent that supports Relay-ID should make it administratively configurable.
sections.eli5: A badge number is only useful if it does not keep changing. If a helper is swapped out, the new helper should be able to wear the same badge.

sections.title: Making Identifiers Unique
sections.content:
A Relay-ID configured in a relay agent MUST be unique within its administrative domain. If it is not, the server may try to allocate the same resource to devices behind two different relay agents. To help, relay agents SHOULD make their identifiers visible to administrators through a user interface, a log entry, a MIB field or another mechanism.

The RFC lists several strategies, and says the list is not exhaustive:

  • Reuse an identifier that is already guaranteed to be unique, such as a UUID (RFC 4122).
  • Use a provisioning system that enumerates relay agents by role and assigns roles to devices, so a replacement relay can take over the role of the one it replaces.
  • Use server event notification on duplicate Relay-IDs, so an administrator can work out whether the duplicate is a mistake or a replacement.
  • Have a management system collect all relay agents and flag any that report the same Relay-ID.
sections.eli5: Two helpers wearing the same badge number would confuse everyone. So the grown-ups need a way to hand out numbers that never repeat and to notice mix-ups.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Relay Agent Information option depends on a trusted relationship between relay agent and server (RFC 3046, RFC 4030). A perimeter defense can block these options unless the relay is trusted. The RFC says a deeper defense using the authentication sub-option (RFC 4030) SHOULD be deployed as well, which also helps stop malicious entities from duplicating relay identifiers. Supporting that authentication sub-option is not required in order to support Relay-ID.

The factory-floor scenario carries a physical risk. If a relay agent has an incorrect Relay-ID, devices could be misconfigured in a way that produces incorrect results, causes physical damage, or creates hazardous conditions for workers. Administrators must use some dependable technique to prevent this. As an example, a relay could require a hardware token holding its Relay-ID, attached to the installation location, and refuse to relay DHCP packets until the token is connected. A relay device with no clear mitigation for such a scenario should not be deployed in it.
sections.eli5: If a helper wears the wrong badge in a factory, a machine might get the wrong instructions, which could be dangerous. So the badge should be locked to the place it belongs.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA assigned a new sub-option code from the "DHCP Relay Agent Sub-Option Codes" registry: the Relay Agent Identifier Sub-Option is code 12.
sections.eli5: The number 12 was officially written down in the list of badge types so nobody else uses it for something different.

fields.name: length
fields.desc: Octets in the sub-option, excluding code and length; minimum one.

fields.name: identifier (variable)
fields.desc: The identifying data, of variable length.
